newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ power poised for second wave of rationalisation.
newsitem.headline: NZ power poised for second wave of rationalisation.

text.p: New Zealand's power sector is in for a second wave of rationalisation if a proposed deal between Power New Zealand, UtiliCorp United Inc and Mercury Energy proceeds as planned, analysts said on Monday.
They said the action would likely centre on the upper North Island, where operators stood to benefit from either mergers or acquisitions via greater economies of scale.
Deregulation in power distribution started apace in 1993, and was followed by a flurry of mergers and acquisitions.
But a hiatus followed when the number of available companies dried up.
"We've had a whole round of initial acquisitions and sometimes they've been priced aggressively," said Paul Richardson, energy analyst at brokers SBC Warburg.
Those acquisitions had taken time to "bed down" through a process of rationalisation and simplification of things like billing structures.
"So you're probably going to see another round of activity anyway, even without this particular trigger," Richardson said.

Continued pressure from Minister of Energy John Luxton for companies to get their tariffs down may put additional pressure on corporates to cut costs, and more "friendly" mergers or joint ventures may be a way to achieve that, analysts said.
However, a potential obstacle to further rationalisation might be the government's coalition agreement, which insists on public approval before privatisation of publically owned assets.
Kansas-based UtiliCorp, though UtiliCorp New Zealand Ltd, finally got together with Mercury on May 20 to bury the hatchet.

Their deal involves combining each one's major shareholding to form a single 64 percent block -- and an offer to minorities at NZ$6.0 a share. The result would be 50/50 ownership of Power NZ through a Mercury-UtiliCorp joint venture.
A quasi-union of Auckland's Mercury and neighbouring Power NZ would see synergistic benefits for both parties.
It would also free Mercury, which plans to list next year, to look at other acquisitions, analysts said.

Longer term, it opens up the prospect of Mercury achieving what it has wanted all along -- a full marriage of the Auckland entities as one company, minus Power NZ's Valley Power assets to the south, which would be divested.
Mercury has long held that Valley Power would be better off being part of a regional central North Island grouping.
UtiliCorp also has ancilliary investments in region, with 39.5 percent of Hamilton's WEL Energy. Through Power NZ, it has 52.5 percent of Whakatane-based based Bay of Plenty Electricity.
Bay of Plenty, WEL Energy, UtiliCorp and Power NZ have made no secret that they like Tauranga-based TrustPower.

Analysts said a TrustPower-WEL Energy mix would appear to be a natural fit, but the sticking point would be the WEL Energy Trust, which has 43 percent of WEL, and which is known to oppose foreign control. TrustPower is also anti- foreign control.
"In both examples the trusts are the dominant shareholders, so I wonder if somehow they can get their interests together like that," said one analyst, who declined to be identified.

"There are three or four companies in that region that logically need to merge or be taken over. BOP needs to merge with somebody, probably TrustPower," said the analyst. "Several of the fringe companies would probably come afterwards."
If the deal proceeds, a Mercury-Power NZ tie-up would form a formidable force, with combined market share of 22 percent.
Mercury, as a super utility, would change the balance of power within the entire sector.
A regional combine of the smaller southern utilities formed around Hamilton and Tauranga would also create a strong player.
"After this, you've got some companies that are at their maximum size for the New Zealand market. There is no way they're getting any bigger other than through mergers," said another analyst.
